# Introduction

This report generates the results reported in our paper (but not the figures---see the script `final_paper_figures.R` for those).


```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 5,
                      fig.height = 3,
                      out.width = "75%",
                      message = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center")
options(list(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE))
theme_set( theme_classic() )

source( here::here( "empirical/load_and_prep_empirical_results.R" ) )

```


# Some statistics on the studies

Our count of studies is the following:
```{r}
whole_studies <- studies %>%
  group_by( Project,Collection, blocked ) %>%
  summarise( n = n() )
table( whole_studies$Collection, whole_studies$blocked ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

Our count of outcomes is the following:

```{r}
table( studies$Collection, studies$blocked ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```


Some statistics about the blocked studies across the `r nrow(filter( studies, blocked=="Blocked"))` outcomes they entail:
```{r}
studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked" ) %>%
  pivot_longer( c( n, ncv, nbar, J, Jcv, K, cluster_ICC, block_ICC,
                   R2.1, R2.2, p.tx, R_ate, R_se ),
                names_to="statistic", values_to="value" ) %>%
  group_by( statistic ) %>%
  summarise( mean = mean(value),
             median = median( value ),
             sd = sd(value),
             min = min( value ),
             Q10 = quantile(value, 0.1),
             Q90 = quantile(value, 0.9),
             max = max( value ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

```

The `R_ate` and `R_se` are the ranges of ATE estimates and the ratios of SE estimates (across estimator); more on those below.


**The 10th and 90th percentile number of individuals, clusters and blocks are around: 850 to 17,500 (individuals), 30 to 495 (clusters), and 5 to 85 (blocks).**

```{r}
blocked = filter( studies, blocked =="Blocked" )

n = quantile( blocked$n, c(0.1, 0.9) )
J = quantile( blocked$J, c(0.1, 0.9) )
K = quantile( blocked$K, c(0.1, 0.9) )
bind_rows( n=n, J=J, K=K, .id = "unit" ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```





## Which studies have singletons and doubletons?

This table lists the number of singletons and doubletons for the Blocked experiments
```{r}
studies %>% 
  dplyr::filter( blocked == "Blocked" ) %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, num_singletons, num_doubletons ) %>% 
  knitr::kable(  )
```

We can tally the outcomes by study type.
Many of the studies had at least one singleton:
```{r}
studies %>% 
  group_by( blocked, Collection ) %>%
  summarise( n_outcome = n(),
             n_no_singletons = sum( num_singletons == 0 ),
             n_no_doubletons = sum( num_doubletons == 0 ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```



## Studies with low degrees of freedom

In this report, we define "Low" to be strictly less than 10 degrees of freedom, with degrees of freedom defined as
$$ df_{cons} =  J - 2K - 1 $$
Here are all studies with 30 or fewer "conservative" degrees of freedom (so low and near low):


```{r}
studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked", cons_df <= 30 ) %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, cons_df, n, J, K, Jbar, Jcv, ncov.1, ncov.2 ) %>%
  arrange( cons_df ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

# Some statistics on our estimators

For each outcome we calculate a bunch of ATE estimates and SE estimates.
We then look at the range of ATE estimates and the ratio of the max to min SE estimate.

We can then tally the number of outcomes with a large ranges of SE (2x or more) and/or ATE (0.10 or more):

```{r}
studies %>% 
  filter( blocked == "Blocked" ) %>%
  group_by( big_ate, big_se ) %>%
  summarise( n = n() ) %>%
  mutate( big_ate = ifelse( big_ate == "", "No", "Yes" ),
          big_se = ifelse( big_se == "", "No", "Yes" )
          ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```


## How often the ATE range is large

Here we count the number of ranges greater than 0.10 and 0.05:

```{r}
ranges %>%
  group_by( group, measure ) %>%
  filter( str_detect( measure, "ate") ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_10 = sum( Range >= 0.10 ),
             big_10 = n_10 / n,
             n_05 = sum( Range >= 0.05 ),
             big_5 = n_05 / n ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

```

## How often estimated Standard error ratio is large

The `n_1.2`, etc are the number of outcomes with a ratio of that amount or larger.  The "big" is just the percent of outcomes.

```{r}
ranges %>%
  group_by( group, measure ) %>%
  filter( !str_detect( measure, "ate") ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
              n_1.2 = sum( Range >= 1.2 ),
             big_1.2 = n_1.2 / n,
            n_1.5 = sum( Range >= 1.5 ),
             big_1.5 = n_1.5 / n,
             n_2 = sum( Range >= 2 ),
             big_2 = n_2 / n,
             max = max( Range ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

```

## Stability connected to df

Here we divide our outcomes by low vs high degree of freedom, and then count how many ratios are large vs. small within those subgroups:

```{r}
ranges %>%
  group_by( low_df, group, measure ) %>%
  filter( !str_detect( measure, "ate") ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_1.2 = sum( Range >= 1.2 ),
             big_1.2 = n_1.2 / n,
             n_1.5 = sum( Range >= 1.5 ),
             big_1.5 = n_1.5 / n,
             n_2 = sum( Range >= 2 ),
             big_2 = n_2 / n ) %>%
  arrange( group, measure, desc(low_df) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

```


We can also make a quick boxplot to show the difference in ratio by low vs high df:

```{r}
ranges %>%
  filter( measure == "ate" | measure == "se" ) %>%
  ggplot( aes( low_df, Range ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ measure, scales="free" ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "Ratio/Range under different specifications" )

ggsave( file="range_boxplot.pdf", width = 5, height = 2 )
```

And singleton vs not:

```{r}
ranges %>%
  filter( measure == "ate" | measure == "se" ) %>%
  ggplot( aes( has_single, Range ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ measure, scales="free" ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "Ratio/Range for studies with and without singletons" )

```




## When are SE estimators defined?

In the paper we write about how singletons make SEs undefined, and how we can run out of degrees of freedom if we adjust for too many covariates.
To support this, the following table counts the number of undefined estimates for each estimator, for different sets of baselind covariates included.

```{r}
#cc <- combined %>%
#  dplyr::select( UniqueID, Covariates, Estimator, ATE_hat_std, SE_hat_std )
#skimr::skim( cc )
combined %>%
  group_by( Covariates, Estimator ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_ATE = sum( is.na( ATE_hat_std ) ),
             n_SE = sum( is.na( SE_hat_std ) ) ) %>%
  pivot_wider( names_from=Covariates, values_from=c(n_ATE, n_SE) ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

The next table counts the number of estimates for each **outcome** that are undefined (the different columns correspond to adjusting for all covariates, a single best covariate, or no covariates):

```{r}
combined %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, Covariates ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_ATE = sum( is.na( ATE_hat_std ) ),
             n_SE = sum( is.na( SE_hat_std ) ) ) %>%
  pivot_wider( names_from=Covariates, values_from=c(n_ATE, n_SE) ) %>%
  dplyr::select( -n_ATE_none ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

Note for no covariate adjustment, we see that 8 estimators will not give SEs for the studies that have singletons (we have 8 of those estimators).

So these two tables count undefined-ness first by estimator and then by outcome.

## What is the average range and ratio?

The following table shows the average range (for ATEs) and average ratio (for estimated SEs) across all our outcomes:

This tells us, for example, that "On average, the largest standard error is around 33% larger than the smallest, across studies."
This is for the "best" covariate adjustment:

```{r}
ranges %>%
  dplyr::filter( Covariates == "best" ) %>%
  dplyr::filter( !str_detect( measure, "noFI" ) ) %>%
  group_by( group, Estimand, measure ) %>%
  summarise( avg = mean( Range ),
             sd = sd( Range ),
             Q05 = quantile( Range, 0.05 ),
             Q95 = quantile( Range, 0.95 ),
             n = sum( !is.na(Range) ) ) %>%
  arrange( measure, group, Estimand ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```


## ATE range and SE ratios vs study characteristics

We can see if  our "conservative df" for each study predicts the range of point estimates or ratio of SE estimates. We top-code all studies with 30 df or more to 30 to make the plots easier to read.

```{r}
ranges %>%
  filter( group=="all" ) %>%
  mutate( cons_df_adj = ifelse( cons_df > 30, 30, cons_df ) ) %>%
ggplot( aes(cons_df_adj, Range ) ) +
  #facet_grid(  measure ~ has_single, scales="free" ) +
  facet_wrap(  ~ measure, scales="free" ) +
  geom_jitter( aes( col=has_single  ), height=0, width=0.5 ) +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE) +
  geom_smooth( aes( col=has_single  ), method="lm", se=FALSE)
```

Commentary: This plot does show there is some tendency for ranges and ratios to go down as DF goes up, but there is a lot of variation around that tendency.


We next look at the distribution of range/ratio of estimates across outcome, grouping by singleton status.  We see the studies with singletons tend to have smaller ATE ranges, and the range of SE estimates is marginally higher---note that the singleton studies SE ratios are over fewer estimators (none of the FI estimators are defined), which would generally push the ratios _lower_ as there are fewer points to take the max and min from.


```{r, fig.height=2}
ranges %>%
  filter( group=="all" ) %>%
  mutate( cons_df_adj = ifelse( cons_df > 30, 30, cons_df ) ) %>%
ggplot( aes(has_single, Range ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ measure, scales="free_x" ) +
  geom_boxplot()  +
  coord_flip()
```

Commentary: I am not sure if these plots are useful or informative.
I am not sure what they mean, either.

# Variation in the ATE Estimates

## Studies with a high range (more than 0.15) of ATE estimates

```{r}
ss <- studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked", R_ate > 0.15 ) %>%
  dplyr::select( Project, UniqueID, K, J, n, cons_df, R_ate, R_ate_Clu, R_ate_Per )

ss %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```


## Range within Estimand

If we go within study, we get the following average reduction in the ATE range when we go to within estimand from overall:

```{r}
# Looking at how range decreases as we go within estimand
source( here::here( "empirical/calculate_all_ranges.R" ) )
ss <- summary_stats_estimand %>%
  filter(Covariates == "best") %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, Estimand, Range ) 
#ss
ss1 <- summary_stats %>%
  filter(Covariates == "best") %>%
  dplyr::select(UniqueID, Range)
ssf <- left_join(ss, ss1, by = 'UniqueID')

ssf %>% 
  mutate( reduction = Range.x / Range.y,
          del = Range.y - Range.x ) %>%
  group_by( Estimand ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             mean_reduction = mean( reduction ),
             sd_reduction = sd( reduction ),
             cor = cor( reduction, Range.y ),
             mean_del = mean(del) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits=2 )
```

We see a notable drop in the ranges when we go to "within estimand" from "overall."

We can plot the ranges within vs. between:

```{r}
ggplot( ssf, aes( Range.y, Range.x, color=Estimand ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Estimand ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline( slope=1, intercept=0, lty="dashed" ) +
  labs( title = "ATE Range within Estimand vs Overall ATE Range",
        x = "Overall ATE Range",
        y = "Within Estimand ATE Range" ) +
  coord_fixed()
```


If we look at all studies with an ATE range above 0.10 for any estimand, we get the following list:

```{r}
ss <- studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked", R_ate > 0.10 | R_ate_Clu > 0.10 | R_ate_Per > 0.10 ) %>%
  dplyr::select( Project, UniqueID, K, J, n, cons_df, R_ate, R_ate_Clu, R_ate_Per )

ss %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

Some statistics on the selected studies:
```{r}
cc <- combined %>%
  dplyr::filter( UniqueID %in% ss$UniqueID, Covariates == "best" ) 

cc %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, num_singletons, ncv, Jcv ) %>% 
  summarise( ATE_min = min( ATE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             ATE_max = max( ATE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             range = ATE_max - ATE_min,
             SE_avg = mean( SE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             n_est = n(),
             n_def = sum( !is.na( ATE_hat_std ) ) ) %>%
  arrange( UniqueID ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```


```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6, out.width= "100%" }

ggplot( cc, aes(Estimator, ATE_hat_std, color = Estimand ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ UniqueID, scales="free_x", nrow=1 ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point( data=filter(cc,str_detect( Estimator, "MLM" ) ), 
              color="black", shape = 21, size = 3 ) +
  coord_flip() +
    theme(panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines"))
```

Note: The MLM estimators are circled to indicate they are not unbiased for either estimand, in principle.

## What predicts range within estimand

Extending the overall plots from above, we can look at what study characteristics drive larger or smaller ranges, within estimand:

```{r}
rr <- rangesW %>%
  filter( Covariates =="best", group=="estimand" ) %>%
  mutate( cons_df_adj = ifelse( cons_df > 30, 30, cons_df ) ) 

ggplot( rr, aes(cons_df_adj, Range, col=has_single ) ) +
  facet_wrap( . ~ Estimand,  nrow=1 ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE) +
  labs( title = 'Range of ATE estimates within estimand' )
```

Range does go up as expected with average SE increasing:
```{r}
rr %>%
ggplot( aes(SE_avg, Range, color=has_single ) ) +
  facet_wrap( . ~ Estimand,  nrow=1 ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE)

```


## Does variation in cluster size or number of clusters predict range?

We can see if range depends on variation in block or cluster size:
```{r}
rr2 <- rangesW %>%
  filter( Covariates =="best", group=="all" ) %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, cons_df, ncv, Jcv, Range ) %>%
  pivot_longer( c( ncv, Jcv ), names_to="var_type", values_to="var_value" )
#rr2

ggplot( rr2, aes(var_value, Range ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ var_type ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE) +
  labs( title = "Range of ATE estimates vs variation in cluster size (ncv) or number of clusters (Jcv)" )
```

We do see the range go up as cluster size variation goes up, but not so much with number of clusters variation.

Within estimand, we can do the same as above (I dropped the extreme outlier above 1 for better visualization and more robust trend detection):

```{r}
rr3 <- rangesW %>%
  filter( Covariates =="best", 
          group =="estimand" ) %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, Estimand, cons_df, ncv, Jcv, SE_avg, Range ) %>%
  pivot_longer( c( ncv, Jcv ), names_to="var_type", values_to="var_value" ) %>%
  filter( UniqueID != "jg_crt_2" )

ggplot( rr3, aes(var_value, Range ) ) +
  facet_grid( Estimand ~ var_type ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE) +
   labs( title = "Range of ATE estimates vs variation in cluster size (ncv) or number of clusters (Jcv)",
         subtitle = "Within Estimand",
         caption = "Outlier with high ncv removed" )
```

Within estimand, we see the same pattern with cluster size variation, but not number of clusters variation.


We can use trees to predict what predicts larger range:

```{r}
rr2 <- rangesW %>%
  filter( Covariates =="best", group=="all" )

source( here::here( "analysis/R/create_analysis_tree.R" ) )
tree1<-create_analysis_tree(rr2,
                            "Range",
                            predictor_vars = c( "cons_df", "ncv", "Jcv", "SE_avg", "R2.1", "R2.2", "has_single", "cluster_ICC", "block_ICC" ) )
```

Big SE means big ranges.
If we drop the average SE as a predictive feature, we get this:
```{r}
set.seed( 40440 )
tree1<-create_analysis_tree(rr2,
                            "Range",
                            predictor_vars = c( "cons_df", "ncv", "Jcv", "R2.1", "R2.2",
                                                "has_single", "cluster_ICC", "block_ICC" ) )
```

These trees shows that uncertainty drives larger differences, and also that greater variation in cluster size drives larger differences, especially if there is variation in the cluster means.

If we look within estimand (i.e., fit our tree to the full set of 50 person ranges and 50 cluster ranges), we see that our datasets with larger R2.1 and no singletons have larger ranges (assuming the SEs are generally large):

```{r}
tree2<-create_analysis_tree(rr,
                            "Range",
                            predictor_vars = c( "cons_df", "Estimand", "ncv", "Jcv",
                                                "SE_avg", "R2.1", "R2.2", "has_single",
                                                "cluster_ICC", "block_ICC" ) )

```

## Comparing low DF to high DF studies

We can look to see if studies with high or low df have generally larger ranges:

```{r}
ra <- rr2 %>%
  group_by( low_df ) %>%
  summarise( avg_rng = mean( Range ),
             sd_rng = sd( Range ),
             Q05 = quantile( Range, 0.05 ),
             Q95 = quantile( Range, 0.95 ),
             n = n() )
ra$ratio = ra$avg_rng / min( ra$avg_rng )

ra %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

The low df studies tend to have higher ranges than the high df studies.
Low df studies also are higher uncertainty studies, so this makes sense.

# Variation in the Estimated Standard Errors


## Studies with a high ratio of SE estimates


Here are all the studies with a min-max SE ratio above 1.5.

```{r}
CUT = 1.5
ss <- studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked", R_se > CUT | R_se_Clu > CUT | R_se_Per > CUT ) %>%
  dplyr::select( Project, UniqueID, K, J, n, cons_df, R_se, R_se_Clu, R_se_Per )

ss %>%
  arrange( UniqueID ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

Some extra info on these studies:
```{r}
combined %>%
  dplyr::filter( UniqueID %in% ss$UniqueID, Covariates == "best" ) %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, cons_df, num_singletons ) %>% 
  summarise( SE_min = min( SE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             SE_max = max( SE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             n_est = n(),
             n_def = sum( !is.na( SE_hat_std ) ) ) %>%
  arrange( UniqueID ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 4 )
```

The individual SE estimates for the troublesome studies:

```{r, out.width="100%", fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
  stud <- combined |>
    filter(UniqueID %in% ss$UniqueID, !is.na(SE_hat_std), Covariates =="best" ) |>
    mutate(
        MLM = ifelse( str_detect( Estimator, "MLM" ), "MLM", "" ),
        EE = factor( paste0( Estimand, MLM ),
                     levels = c( "Person", "ClusterMLM", "Cluster" ) ),
      Estimator = factor(Estimator),
      Estimator = fct_reorder(Estimator, as.numeric( EE ), .na_rm = TRUE)
    )
agg <- stud %>% 
  group_by( UniqueID, EE ) %>%
  summarise( SE_hat_std = mean( SE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ) ) %>%
  filter( EE != "ClusterMLM" )

  ggplot(stud, aes(Estimator, SE_hat_std, pch=EE, col = EE)) +
    facet_wrap( ~ UniqueID ) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_hline( yintercept = 0 ) +
    geom_hline( aes( yintercept = SE_hat_std, col=EE ), data=agg, lty=2 ) +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
      title = "SE estimates",
      subtitle = "(For defined estimators)"
    )

```

## How often are the SE estimates defined?

Here we look at 'best' and see how often the SE estimates are defined for each outcome.
We see that for 34 outcomes, 57% of our estimators are defined and for 16 outcomes all of them are defined.

```{r}
cc <- combined %>%
  filter( Covariates == "best" ) %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, Covariates ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_def = sum( !is.na( SE_hat_std ) ),
             per_def = n_def / n, .groups = "drop" )

table( cc$Covariates, cc$per_def )

```

## How much do SE ratios go down within Estimand?

In the following we look at how much the SE ratios shrink going within estimand.

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Looking at how range decreases as we go within estimand
source( here::here( "empirical/calculate_all_ranges.R" ) )
ss <- summary_stats_estimand %>%
  filter(Covariates == "best") %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, Estimand, Ratio ) 
#ss
ss1 <- summary_stats %>%
  filter(Covariates == "best") %>%
  dplyr::select(UniqueID, Ratio)
ssf <- left_join(ss, ss1, by = 'UniqueID')

ssf %>% 
  mutate( rat = Ratio.x / Ratio.y ) %>%
  group_by( Estimand ) %>%
  summarise( mean_reduction = mean( rat ),
             sd_reduction = sd( rat ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits=2 )
  
#knitr::kable( ssf, digits = 2 )
```

Overall, we are not seeing much of a reduction in the max/min SE ratio by going from overall to within.

We can look at the individual reductions:

```{r}
  ggplot( ssf, aes( Ratio.y, Ratio.x ) ) +
    facet_wrap( ~ Estimand ) +
    geom_point() +
    coord_fixed() +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, lty = 2, col = 'red') +
    labs( x = "Overall ratio", y = "Within Estimand Ratio" )
```



# Are SEs for cluster weight smaller than individual?

We might think the SEs for cluster-weighted estimands might be systematically larger than those for individual-weighted estimands.
We check this on the empirical estimates.

To investigate, we fit a multilevel model to our raw estimated standard errors, having a random intercept for the outcome and for the estimator.
We also allow for a "random slope" for estimand within outcome, as it is possible that some studies are better at targeting person vs cluster average effects.
We finally allow a random slope by estimator for studies with singletons, to see if some estimators have estimated SEs that change more depending on whether there are singletons present.
We further adjust for aspects of the study.  Our main coefficient is the coefficient for Estimand:

```{r}
library( lme4 )

combined$Covariates = factor( combined$Covariates,
                              levels = c( "best", "none", "all" ) )
M = lmer( log( SE_hat_std ) ~ Estimand + Covariates + has_single + I(log(1+cons_df)) + I(log(nbar)) + I(log(J)) + (1+has_single|Estimator) + (1+Estimand|UniqueID),
          data=combined )
arm::display(M)
```

We see no evidence that targeting person estimands is different from cluster estimands in terms of precision.
There is some variation in average uncertainty by estimator.
The random slope standard deviation of 0.02 suggests some studies might have a difference between person and cluster.

We can look at the exponentiated coefficients to see the multiplicative effect on the SE:
```{r}
exp( fixef( M ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

This suggests that person-weighted is 3% more precise (but the result is not statistically significant).

We can use a LR test to see if there is evidence of variation by study:

```{r}
Mnull = lmer( log( SE_hat_std ) ~ Estimand + Covariates + has_single + I(log(1+cons_df)) + I(log(nbar)) + I(log(J)) + (1+has_single|Estimator) + (1|UniqueID),
          data=combined, REML=FALSE )
anova( M, Mnull )
```

No evidence of variation.


## Analysis: What drives overall uncertainty?

Our model, above, tells us more about what drives overall uncertainty.

For example, relative to 'best', not controlling for any baseline covariates means estimated SEs are 17% larger.
Controlling for everything makes the estimated SEs 10% smaller.
Bigger studies in terms of either n or J have smaller SEs, as expected.
The estimated SEs for the studies with singletons are generally smaller; it is unclear what that is coming from.

We can dig into which estimators are better or worse, in terms of their estimated SEs, by looking at the Empirical Bayes estimates of their random intercepts:

```{r}
ranef(M)$Estimator %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column(var="estimator" ) %>%
  rename( avg = `(Intercept)`,
          singletons = has_singlesingetons ) %>%
  mutate( avg = exp(avg),
          singletons = exp( singletons ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

The estimators have no variation in the average estimated SE, but do differ when faced with studies with singletons.
In particular, MLM-FIcw is 6% larger, and LRicw-FE-crve is 12% smaller---the latter is likely due to poorly estimated CRVEs when there are singletons.



## Which estimators tend to be most extreme?

Here we tag when each estimator is either the 1st or second smallest or 1st or second largest SE estimate of all availables for that outcome (within the "best" covariate set).

```{r}
extreme <- combined %>%
  filter( Covariates == "best", !is.na( SE_hat_std ) ) %>%
  group_by( UniqueID ) %>%
  mutate( ratio = max( SE_hat_std ) / min(SE_hat_std ),
          extreme = rank( SE_hat_std, ties.method = "first" ) <= 2 |
          rank( SE_hat_std, ties.method = "first" ) >= n() - 1 ) %>%
  filter( ratio > 1.25 ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by( Estimator, Estimand ) %>%
  summarise( n_def = n(),
             n_extreme = sum( extreme ),
             per = n_extreme / n_def )

extreme %>%
  arrange( per ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )


```

The `n_def` column is the number of outcomes where the estimator was even defined.

I'm not sure this table is particularly informative, but it does show that some estimators are more likely to be extreme than others.  The problem is some estimators aren't even defined, which robs them of the opportunity to be informative.


\newpage

# How do covariates move the point estimates?

We next look at how much the point estimates change as we adjust for more covariates (all) or no covariates (none) vs. our baseline of "best".
For each outcome and estimator we calculated the difference between the ATE estimate when controlling for the single best covariate, and the ATE estimate when controlling for nothing ("none") or all available covariates ("all").
We subset to the core estimators, removing redundancies and similar estimators

The first plot shows the scatterplot of the "best" ATE estimate vs. the "all" or "none" ATE estimate, faceted by estimator.
The second plot shows the distribution of the difference between the "best" ATE estimate and the "all" or "none" ATE estimate, again grouped by estimator.

```{r, out.width="100%", warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=8}
cc1 <- combined %>%
  filter( !is.na( ATE_hat_std ) ) %>%
  pivot_wider( id_cols = c( UniqueID, Estimator, Estimand ),
               names_from = Covariates,
               values_from = ATE_hat_std ) %>%
  pivot_longer( c( all, none ),
                names_to = "Covariates",
                values_to = "ATE_hat" ) %>%
  rename(ATE_hat_best = best ) %>%
  mutate( diff = ( ATE_hat - ATE_hat_best ) ) 
#cc1
  
core.methods <- c("LRa-FE-db", "LRa-FIcw-db", 
                  "LRi-FE-db", "LRi-FIpw-db", 
                  "MLM-RE", "MLM-FIcw" )

cc1 <- cc1 %>%
  dplyr::filter( Estimator %in% core.methods )

ggplot( cc1, aes( ATE_hat_best, ATE_hat ) ) +
  #facet_grid( Estimand ~ Covariates ) +
  geom_abline( slope=1, intercept=0, col="red", alpha=0.5 ) +
  facet_grid( Covariates ~ Estimator ) +
  geom_point( size=0.5 ) +
  coord_fixed()


ggplot( cc1, aes( Estimator, diff ) ) +
  #facet_grid( Estimand ~ Covariates ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Covariates  ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = c(-0.10,0.10), lty="dashed", col="red" ) +
  coord_flip()
```

The plot above shows that, while generally adjusting for covariates does not change the estimate much, it can move a point estimate a very large amount.  (The red lines are at 0.10 and -0.10.)

We can then look at shifts by study, rather than by estimator:

```{r estplot, fig.height=8, fig.width=6, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%"}

ggplot( cc1, aes( UniqueID, diff ) ) +
  #facet_grid( Estimand ~ Covariates ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Covariates  ) +
  geom_boxplot( size=0.5 ) +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_hline( yintercept = 0, col="red" ) +
  labs( title = "Shift in ATE estimate vs. 'best' adjustment" )
```

We see some studies tend to have large impacts of adjustment across the estimators, and other studies not so much, regardless of estimator.

We can summarize average differences by estimator and adjustment:

```{r}
cc1 %>%
  group_by( Estimator, Estimand, Covariates ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             avg_diff = mean( abs(diff), na.rm=TRUE ),
             sd_diff = sd( abs(diff), na.rm=TRUE ),
             Q10 = quantile( abs(diff), 0.1,  na.rm=TRUE ),
             Q90 = quantile( abs(diff), 0.9, na.rm=TRUE ) ) %>%
  arrange( Estimand, Estimator ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```


We can see if the size of the change in point estimate is related to the overall uncertainty in the study:

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
rra <- rangesW %>%
  dplyr::filter( group == "all", Covariates=="best" ) %>%
  dplyr::select( -Estimand, -Covariates )

cc2 <- left_join( cc1, 
                  rra, 
                  by="UniqueID" )
#cc2
#cc2$cons_df = cc2$J - 2*cc2$K - 1
cc2$cons_df <- ifelse( cc2$cons_df > 30, 30, cc2$cons_df )

ggplot( cc2, aes( cons_df, abs(diff) ) ) +
  facet_grid( Covariates ~ Estimator  ) +
  geom_point(size=0.5)+
  geom_smooth( method="lm", se=FALSE )

ggplot( cc2, aes( SE_avg, abs(diff) ) ) +
  facet_grid( Covariates ~ Estimator  ) +
  geom_point(size=0.5)+
  geom_smooth( method="lm", se=FALSE )

```

These features do not seem to explain when covariate adjustment matters a lot.

Here are the studies where there was massive change (above 0.15) when adjusting for covariates for at least one estimator:


```{r}
cc2 %>%
  filter( abs(diff) >= 0.15 ) %>%
  arrange( desc( abs(diff) ) ) %>%
    group_by( Covariates, UniqueID, cons_df, J, K, nbar, R2.1, R2.2 ) %>%
  summarise( n_est = n(),
             avg_diff = mean(abs(diff) ) ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange( Covariates, -avg_diff ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

`n_est` is the number of estimators where the adjustment was bigger than 0.15.
